candidates.text:
May the divine Waters be auspicious to us for our succour, auspicious for us to drink; may they flow about us bringing well-being and ease.
O Waters, fill me full of healing medicine, a shelter for my body; and may I long behold the sun.
Soma declared to me that within the Waters are all remedies, and Agni who brings well-being to all.
Ruling over precious things, dwelling among the peoples — from the Waters I beg healing medicine.
The mothers — kinswomen who minister at the sacrifice — travel along their paths, mingling the milk with honey.
Those yonder that are near the sun, and those with whom the sun moves together — may they speed our sacrifice.
I call upon the divine Waters where our cows drink; an oblation is to be made to the rivers.
Within the Waters is immortality, within the Waters is medicine; and in the praises of the Waters, O horses, you become vigorous steeds.

He whom the three — gods, men, and all cattle — follow in their going: may the divine mind speak on our behalf for him; may good guidance lead us; may we not fall prey to the enemy.
Splendorous art thou among the gods, splendorous among the plants. Now make splendorous the one upon whom, O Aśvattha, thou dost climb.
The Aśvattha has ascended over him who is king of the human folk. Like Indra he smites down foes; may the kingship not be dislodged from him.
Āroha by name thou art; thou hast arisen with might. May this man carry thee, O Aśvattha, crusher of rivals.
Thou art king of all beings, the bull, the lord of plants. O Aśvattha, scatter our rivals asunder in all directions.
Looking upon one another they came for immortality, pure ones being born forth from their wombs. Making auspicious augury, smell this one here; place this hero among heroes.

That which is born from the north, the madhugha plant, born from the madhugha — in it I know the remedy. My tongue is full of sweetness.
Sweet is your leaf, O plant, sweet your horns and your blossom. Sweet was the mountain from which you were born, O herb.
You are the embryo of the plants, and you were the embryo of the waters. Moreover, you are the brother of Soma — O madhugha, promote my speech.
For good fortune I have grasped the name of the madhugha plant as one grasps a father's name — may it make me brilliant as gold, beloved of men.
Make me dear among the gods, make me dear among kings. Make me dear in the sight of all who look — both the Śūdra and the Ārya.
Be pleased with the udder, be pleased with the heart, be pleased with the mouth and the tongue. Be pleased, O cow swollen full with milk.

This Agni has bewildered all the thoughts that are in your hearts; he blows you away from your dwelling, he blows you forth from every side.
O Indra, confound their minds — draw their very intent hither; with the rushing blast of Agni and of Wind scatter them in all directions and destroy them.
Let their intentions scatter hence, and let their minds be bewildered; and whatever is today within their hearts — that, strike out and expel from them utterly.
Seizing their minds in utter bewilderment, O Apvā, go forth and grasp their limbs; advance, burn them inwardly with grief in their hearts, pierce our foes — those enemies fit to be seized — with darkness.
That army yonder of our adversaries, O Maruts, which advances against us contending with its might — hide it away with darkness and by the hostile rite, so that not one of them may know another.

Soma, the demon-slayer [sharp, sharp-horned, the seer of seers, the poet most poetic — let him thrust away the evil-sayer, overwhelm hostility; back with the counter-stroke: upon the one who works harm, harm we hurl back].
Varuṇa, the demon-slayer [sharp, sharp-horned, the seer of seers, the poet most poetic — let him thrust away the evil-sayer, overwhelm hostility; back with the counter-stroke: upon the one who works harm, harm we hurl back].
Vāyu, the demon-slayer [sharp, sharp-horned, the seer of seers, the poet most poetic — let him thrust away the evil-sayer, overwhelm hostility; back with the counter-stroke: upon the one who works harm, harm we hurl back].
Tvaṣṭā, the demon-slayer [sharp, sharp-horned, the seer of seers, the poet most poetic — let him thrust away the evil-sayer, overwhelm hostility; back with the counter-stroke: upon the one who works harm, harm we hurl back].

Agni, united with the bodies of the waters, who became the lord of the plants — may Jātavedas, the All-knower, win rain for us, the breath of life, the immortal drink, from heaven, for our offspring.
Let lightning flash in every direction; let the winds blow from all quarters. Let the clouds, set in motion by the Maruts, rain down upon the earth.
Prajāpati, stirring up the waters from the primordial flood, from the ocean, agitates the sea. Let the seed of the virile horse swell forth; come hither, our father, the mighty Asura, pouring down the waters with this thunder.
Let the gurgling whirlpools of the waters breathe; send down the waters below. Let the frogs with their speckled arms speak out along the pools.
Having lain dormant for a year, like Brāhmaṇas who observe their vow, the frogs have spoken forth, quickened into voice by Parjanya.

He whose heat poured forth from thy body, dripping gold, pure, following their own nature — here thou dost hold the immortal names; the robes, O master, are set in motion for us.
When these have proclaimed the ancient foremost thing, standing seat by seat on that which ages not — the Sage, as the two Mothers of vitality lick him, has measured the kinsman-bride's form as counterpart.
That great and broad ruling power — the Sage has fashioned it with his wisdom, O Yama, in reverence; when the converging ones press toward the earth, then the great wheel of obstruction has grown.
The seven sages have fashioned the seven bounds; towards one of them the sinful one has gone; yet thou who art immortal in breath, encompassed, advancing, O Asura, attained, goest along by thine own power.

Those who plunge headlong into rivers, clinging together like maidens — of those dog-companied ones, Indra has cut off the head.
Those who wade into fords, hissing like inviolable cows — of those dog-companied ones, Indra has cut off the head.
Those who rise up out of the ocean, uttering loud cries, chattering and clamorous — of those dog-companied ones, Indra has cut off the head.
Those who go from person to person desiring many by the myriad — of those dog-companied ones, Indra has cut off the head.
Agni is long-lived; long-lived is he together with the forest-trees. May he make me long-lived and make this one long-lived.
Vāyu is long-lived; long-lived is he together with the mid-air. May he make me long-lived and make this one long-lived.
Sūrya is long-lived; long-lived is he together with the sky. May he make me long-lived and make this one long-lived.

The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya became his arms; that which is his middle is the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born.
Virāj first came into being; from Virāj the Puruṣa arose; having been born he spread beyond, backward across the earth and also forward.
When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation, spring was its clarified butter, summer its firewood, autumn its oblation.
They sprinkled with the rains that sacrifice, that Puruṣa born in the beginning; with him the gods sacrificed — the Sādhyas and the Vasus.
From him horses were born, and all those that have teeth on both jaws; from him cattle were born, and from him goats and sheep were born.
From that sacrifice offered entire, the Ṛc verses and the Sāman chants were born; the meters were born from it; the Yajus was born from it.

This udumbara amulet, heroic, is bound on for the hero. May it make our acquisition sweet and honeyed, and may it bestow upon us wealth with all its heroes.
May we attain the favour of Bhaga the king, whom human beings invoke in many ways. He who acts in accordance with dharma wins Bhaga as his own — may He make us fortunate among the people.
Awakening to the east, may we behold the divine Dawn shining forth. The bright one facing toward us, bringing Bhaga together with wealth — may Aditi come to us bearing good fortune.
May Bhaga today, at dawn, bestow upon us favour and lead us here along the path of the gods. May auspicious benevolence come toward us; and then may our kindling-fire glow bright with Bhaga.
By Bhaga's impulsion, splendid in lustre, may I speak a speech directed by Sarasvatī, honeyed. May what is given by Bhaga come to me in abundance, so that radiant with lustre I may speak in the assembly.

The sprinkling-water that fell around the sacred grass, south of the altar, charged with vital power — the vaśā-cow lowed above it in full presence; her marrow became her armor-garment.
Homage to your greatness and to your eye, O Vaśā and Ṛṣabha — this I do with the mind. Go together to the gods by auspicious paths; harm us not with divine wrath.
The bull mounted the vaśā-cow as she stood upon the threads of fate. Who today knows that embryo — in what manner he has disposed it?
One encompassed form entire; one is called King by name; one is lord of form, its very form; one is the form of those who act aright.
Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Mṛtyu, Viśvānara, and Svarga — from this sacrifice, from this vaśā, were they born.
In whose house the vaśā were received as an oblation fashioned by the gods — the treasure to be sought of her is like a daughter's to her husband.

O divine Añjana, O Traikakuda, protect me on all sides. Neither the external herbs nor the mountain ones surpass you.
He released the strong middle portion — the destroyer of demons, the disperser of disease. Driving away all diseases, destroying them, the overpowering one expelled them from here.
Much falsehood, O King Varuṇa, has a man spoken. From that, O you of a thousand powers, free us from transgression on every side.
What we have said — \"O inviolable waters,\" \"O Varuṇa\" — from that, O you of a thousand powers, free us from transgression on every side.
May Mitra and Varuṇa follow after you, O Añjana. Having followed you far, may it grow again for enjoyment.
As one debt is discharged by another debt, carry the sorcery back to the house of its maker. O collyrium, O evil-hearted one of the eye-spell, shatter even the ribs.

The divine waters are foremost among the healing herbs. They have driven out the sin-laden yakṣma from your limb by limb.
I address the spreading plants, the clumping ones, the single-stemmed, the creeping herbs. I call you — the filamentous, the jointed, those with spreading branches — those plants that belong to all the gods, the potent, the life-sustaining for man.
By that power of yours, O herbs, which overpowers, by the virile force and strength that is in you — with that, release this man from this yakṣma disease.
I invoke Jīvalā, Naghāriṣā, the living herb, and Arundhatī the uplifting, the flowering one, the honey-sweet one.
May the wise, the knowing ones come here at my word, so that we may carry this man across, beyond misfortune.
The food of Agni, the embryo of the waters — those that grow anew as punarṇavās: may those steadfast, thousand-named healing plants be gathered and brought here.

You are the Low One and you are the Upturned One; in your mouth are Growth and Abundant-Growth. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Rohiṇī and you are Surohiṇī; in your mouth are Food and the Eating-of-Food. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Sarā and you are Sarasvatī; in your mouth are Sacred-Power and Lordly-Might. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.

Those auspicious, gracious forms of thine, O Kāma, by which that which one chooses comes to be true — with those enter into us fully; drive the evil thoughts elsewhere away.
Those two limb-marks which your mother wiped off you at birth — the pativedanau auspices — let not the Evil-Named one covet them there, neither the aliṃśa nor the vatsapa.
The palāla, the anupalāla, the śarkuṇa, the koka, the malimruca, the palījaka, the āśleṣa, the vavrivāsasa, the ṛkṣagrīva, the pramīlina — we smite them away from her pudenda.
Let him not press close, let him not creep up against her thighs, let him not glide between them. I prepare for her this remedy, the baja-plant, banisher of the Evil-Named.
Both the Evil-Named and the Fair-Named desire a woman who is enclosed; we smite away the arāya — the Fair-Named desires what belongs to women.

These indeed — both the beloved and the unloved — are the officiating priests who lead one to the heavenly world, namely the guests (atithis).
When he summons the doorkeeper and causes him to be called, and when he responds and causes the response to be heard in return.
When the servers enter the lodging-places, they are in truth the cup-bearing adhvaryus for those guests — not a single one of them is without the function of an hotṛ.
What one brings forth in the morning — that is verily the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).
What one brings forth at midday — that is verily the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina savana).
What one brings forth in the evening — that is verily the third pressing (tṛtīya savana).
When the lord of the guests, having served the guests all round, asks leave of his seat — he thereby approaches the avabhṛtha (the concluding ablution of the sacrifice).

She on whom the gathering waters flow in their rounds, pouring day and night without ceasing — may that Earth, abundant-streamed, milk nourishment for us, and also sprinkle us with vital radiance.
She whom the gods guard, ever-wakeful, at all times, the Earth, the wide one, without negligence — may she milk sweet, dear nourishment for us, and also sprinkle us with vital radiance.
She who was the primordial waters above the ocean; whom the wise have traced through their visionary powers; she whose heart, in the highest sky, is wrapped in truth, the immortal essence of Earth — may that Earth place brilliance and strength in my realm for me.
She whom the two Aśvins measured out, upon whom Viṣṇu strode; she whom Indra, lord of power, made enemy-free for himself — may that Earth release milk for us as a mother for her son.

These living ones have turned away from the dead; auspicious has been our invocation of the gods today. We have gone forward to dance and to laugh; endowed with good heroes, may we speak in the assembly.
I set this barrier for the living; let no other cross over to this purpose of theirs. May they, living long, traverse many autumns, setting Death aside as if by a mountain.
Just as the days come in succession, just as the seasons go together with the seasons, just as the earlier does not abandon the later — so, O Tvaṣṭṛ, arrange the life-spans of these.
Mount up in life, choosing old age, striving forward in succession wherever you go. May Tvaṣṭṛ of good birth, in harmony with them, lead all their life-span onward to full living.
The stony river flows — take hold, be vigorous, cross over, O friends. Leave behind here those who were of ill will; free from disease, may we rise above to the prizes.

And behold — the rays carry yonder god Jātavedas, the sun, for all the world to see.
Away they go like thieves, as the stars depart through the nights, before the Sun, the all-seeing.
His beams, his rays, have become visible spreading among the peoples, blazing like fires.
Swift, visible to all, maker of light, O Sun — you illuminate all things, shining brilliantly.
Facing the host of gods, facing the races of men, you rise; facing all things you rise to be seen in the sky.
With that purifying eye, O Varuṇa, you behold the bustling peoples moving about.
You traverse the broad sky and the wide atmosphere, measuring out the day with the nights, beholding all created beings, O Sun.
The seven tawny mares carry you on your chariot, O divine Sun — you who have flames for hair, you the far-seeing.

When thou hast matured him, O Jātavedas, then hand him over to the Fathers all around. When this one goes to the guidance of the breath, then he shall become subject to the will of the gods.
Let the eye go to the sun, the breath to the wind; go to heaven and to the earth according to the sacred law. Or go to the waters, if that is thy destiny — take thy stand in the plants with thy bodily parts.
O unborn portion of ascetic heat, blaze upon him; let your flame scorch him, let your fire-ray sear him. O Jātavedas, with those gracious forms of yours, carry him to the world of the well-doers.
Those swift, fierce forms of yours, O Jātavedas, that rush swirling around — let them gather and follow the goat as it goes; then with those other, most benign forms, render him well-cooked and fit.

Whatever vigor is within your hearts, whatever intention has entered your minds — that I attune with oblation and clarified butter; may your delight, O kinsmen, rest in me.
Come to my thought, all of you, at the moment of departure and departure, as to the invocation of Indra and Agni. May Bṛhaspati yoke you to me; be of one mind and follow my speech.
I seize your minds with my mind; come to my thought with your thoughts. I make your hearts subject to my will; come following in my path, come to me.
Let your eye come to me, let your breath come to me; may the Dhātṛ make your path follow my footstep. Whether your elders or your young ones — come, following in my path, come with those who follow.
You were born above the gods; you are placed as a friend of Soma. As such, be gracious for the in-breath, the out-breath, and the sight of this one.

To every being here, and to every one who sees — to all of them I am indeed glorious.
Push away, uncover whatever this is or is not; make the sight blind and impaired — do this to the eyes.
Having made the golden limb, the plow-handle, and the cataract — gods, take that away.
May my mind be possessed of sight, may my heart be possessed of sight; may my consciousness be possessed of sight, may my eye be possessed of sight — place sight in my two eyes.
Soma is king, and Savitā is king, Bhava is king, and the world is king; Śarva is king and Śarman is king — may those gods grant us shelter.
Bṛhaspati with the Ādityas, Bhaga together with Soma, the All-Gods, the wide atmosphere — may those gods grant us shelter.
Strike out the un-pierced one and also loosen the taut one; O All-Gods, O Maruts, do not direct your missile at us.

You are the one that points the way and the one that points it forth. [Prajāpati... may the students of sacred knowledge] come to me. Svāhā!
You are approval and you are the one who grants approval. [Prajāpati... may the students of sacred knowledge] come to me. Svāhā!
You are conquest and you are victory. [Prajāpati... may the students of sacred knowledge] come to me. Svāhā!
You are complete conquest and you are what is won by joining together. [Prajāpati... may the students of sacred knowledge] come to me. Svāhā!
Agni is the lord of the earth; may Soma protect you. We know you; know us. You are the overlord — make me the overlord of cattle, horses, men, students of sacred knowledge, of prosperity and the eating of food.
Vāyu is the lord of the atmosphere; [may Soma protect you. We know you; know us. You are the overlord — make me the overlord of cattle, horses, men, students of sacred knowledge, of prosperity and the eating] of food.

Cry out favourably to us, O owl, and lead away from here the one we hate. In the house of King Yama, your gaming with sand shall be your portion, and a mouse shall nibble it away.
Speak of the plentiful cow-pen, the calf-seeking cow, the cow not lost. Speak of two-footed beings to the crow; speak of four-footed beings to the dog.
May King Varuṇa give back to me again, may Indra give back again, may Bhaga give back again; may all the gods give back to me again life and the means of living.
Rise up, run forward toward us; do not stand gazing here. Having taken the radiance away from the rival wife, then you shall be together with us.
Rise up, run out; there is no descending for you here. I press toward you the wealth of that man yonder — follow it, O fair-toothed ones; the serpent has shed that.

(Enter EUCLIO, driving out STAPHYLA.)
EUCLIO:
Get out, I say, be off, get out; by my troth, you must budge out of this house here, you pryabout woman, with your inquisitive eyes.
STAPHYLA:
Pray why are you beating me, wretched creature that I am?
EUCLIO:
That you may be wretched, and that, curst as you are. you may pass a curst life, well befitting you.
STAPHYLA:
But for what reason have you now pushed me out of the house?
EUCLIO:
Am I to be giving you a reason, you whole harvest of whips. Get away there from the door! There, do look, if you please, how she does creep along. But do you know how matters stand with you? If I just now take a stick or a whip in my hand, I’ll quicken that tortoise pace for you.
STAPHYLA:
O that the Gods would drive me to hang myself, rather indeed than that I should be a slave in your house on these terms!

STAPHYLA:
Keep watch in-doors upon nothing at all, forsooth! or is it, that no one may carry the house away. For here in our house there’s nothing else for thieves to gain, so filled is it with emptiness and cobwebs.
EUCLIO:
’Tis a wonder that, for your sake, Jupiter doesn’t now make me a King Philip, or a Darius, you hag of hags. I choose those cobwebs to be watched for me. I am poor, I confess it—I put up with it. What the Gods send, I endure. Go in-doors, shut to the door, I shall be there directly.
Take you care not to let any strange person into the house.
STAPHYLA:
What if any person asks for fire?
EUCLIO:
I wish it to be put out, that there may be no cause for any one asking it of you. But if the fire shall be kept in, you yourself shall be forthwith extinguished. Then do you say that the water has run out, if any one asks for it.

I think the same, and I’m determined never to contradict you on that point, sister. What do you wish?
EUNOMIA:
Give me your attention, I beg of you.
MEGADORUS:
’Tis at your service; use and command me, please, if you wish for aught.
EUNOMIA:
A thing that I consider very greatly for your advantage
I’m come to recommend you.
MEGADORUS:
Sister, you are doing after your usual manner.
EUNOMIA:
I wish it were done.
MEGADORUS:
What is it, sister?
EUNOMIA:
That you may enjoy everlasting blessings in being the father of children.

EUNOMIA:
And you the same, brother.
(Goes into the house.)
MEGADORUS:
I’ll go meet Euclio, if he’s at home. But, see! the very person is betaking himself home, whence, I know not.
(Enter EUCLIO.)
EUCLIO:
(to himself.)
My mind had a presentiment that I was going to no purpose when I left my house; and therefore I went unwillingly; for neither did any one of the wardsmen come, nor yet the master of the ward, who ought to have distributed the money. Now I’m making all haste to hasten home; for I myself am here, my mind’s at home.
MEGADORUS:
(accosting him.)
May you be well, and ever fortunate, Euclio!
EUCLIO:
May the Gods bless you, Megadorus!
MEGADORUS:
How are you? Are you quite well, and as you wish?

MEGADORUS:
I return you thanks; I beg that as to what I shall enquire of you, you’ll not hesitate to speak out boldly.
EUCLIO:
So long, indeed, as you enquire nothing that I mayn’t choose to speak out upon.
MEGADORUS:
Tell me, of what sort of family do you consider me to be sprung?
EUCLIO:
Of a good one.
MEGADORUS:
What think you as to my character?
EUCLIO:
’Tis a good one.
MEGADORUS:
What of my conduct?
EUCLIO:
Neither bad nor dishonest.

This is the great hazard, in my passing over from the asses to the oxen.
MEGADORUS:
The nearer you can unite yourself in alliance with the virtuous, so much the better. Do you receive this proposal, listen to me, and promise her to me.
EUCLIO:
But indeed there is no marriage-portion.
MEGADORUS:
You are to give none; so long as she comes with good principles, she is sufficiently portioned.
EUCLIO:
I say so for this reason, that you mayn’t be supposing that I have found any treasures.
MEGADORUS:
I know that; don’t enlarge upon it. Promise her to me.
EUCLIO:
So be it. (Starts and looks about.) But, O Jupiter, am I not utterly undone?
MEGADORUS:
What’s the matter with you?
EUCLIO:

(Exit MEGADORUS.)
EUCLIO:
He has gone hence. Immortal Gods, I do beseech you! How powerful is gold! I do believe, now, that he has had some intimation that I’ve got a treasure at home; he’s gaping for that; for the sake of that has he persisted in this alliance.
(EUCLIO, alone.)
EUCLIO:
(going to the door of his house, he opens it, and calls to STAPHYLA within.)
Where are you who have now been blabbing to all my neighbours that I’m going to give a portion to my daughter? Hallo! Staphyla, I’m calling you!
Don’t you hear? Make haste in-doors there, and wash the vessels clean. I’ve promised my daughter in marriage; to-day I shall give her to be married to Megadorus here.
(from the house.)
STAPHYLA:
(as she enters.)
May the Gods bestow their blessings on it! But, i’ faith, it cannot be;’tis too sudden.

ANTHRAX:
And does he stop up the lower part of his windpipe as well, lest, perchance, he should lose any breath as he sleeps?
STROBILUS:
In that’tis as fair that you should credit me, as it is for me to credit you.
ANTHRAX:
Why really, I do believe you.
STROBILUS:
But, further, do you know how it is?
I’ faith, he grieves to throw away the water when he washes.
ANTHRAX:
Do you think a great talent might be begged of this old fellow for him to give us, through which we might become free?
STROBILUS:
By my troth, if you were to ask it, he would never let you have the loan of hunger. Why, the other day, the barber had cut his nails; he collected all the parings, and carried them off.
ANTHRAX:
I’ faith, you do describe a miserably stingy wretch.
LYCONIDES:

LYCONIDES:
I follow.
STROBILUS:
(knocking at the door of EUCLIO’S house.)
Ho, there Staphyla, come out and open the door.
STAPHYLA:
(from within.)
Who calls there?
STROBILUS:
Strobilus.
(Enter STAPHYLA.)
STAPHYLA:
What do you want?
STROBILUS:
For you to take in these cooks, and this music-girl, and these provisions for the wedding. Megadorus bade me take these things to Euclio.
STAPHYLA:

(Goes into the house.)
(Enter EUCLIO, with some chaplets of flowers in his hand.)
EUCLIO:
I wished at length to screw up my courage to-day, so as to enjoy myself at the wedding of my daughter. I come to the market, I enquire about fish; they tell me that it is dear, that lamb is dear, beef is dear, veal, large fish, and pork, all of them are dear. And for this reason were they still dearer; I hadn’t the money. I came away thence in a rage, since I had nothing wherewithal to make a purchase; and thus did I baulk all those rascals. Then I began to think with myself upon the road,
If you are guilty of any extravagance on a festive day, you may be wanting on a common day, unless you are saving. After I disclosed this reasoning to my heart and appetite, my mind came over to my opinion, that I ought to give my daughter in marriage at as little expense as possible.

Why?
EUCLIO:
Because you’ve got a knife.
LYCONIDES:
’Tis the proper thing for a cook.
EUCLIO:
Why did you threaten me?
LYCONIDES:
I think that it was badly managed, that I didn’t pierce your side with it.
EUCLIO:
There’s not a person that’s living this day a greater rascal than you, nor one to whom designedly I would with greater pleasure cause a mischief.
LYCONIDES:
I’ faith, though you should hold your noise, really that’s quite clear; the thing itself is its own witness. As it is, I’m made softer by far with your sticks than any ballet-dancer. But what right have you to touch us, you beggarman? What’s the matter?
EUCLIO:
Do you even ask me? Is it that I’ve done less than I ought to have done? Only let me—
(Is going to strike him.)

LYCONIDES:
Go there yourself then. (CONGRIO and the COOKS and MUSIC-GIRL go back into the house.)
(EUCLIO, alone.)
EUCLIO:
He’s gone. Immortal Gods! A poor man, who begins to have dealings or business with an opulent one, commences upon a rash undertaking! ODE TO CONTENT.
BY J— C—.
CONTENT! who oft art wont to dwell
Deep in the solitary dell,
Near shady wood, or limpid rill,
Or on the side of some hoar hill;
Attendant on the shepherd swain,
Thou cheer'st his labours on the plain.
With thee, he pleas'd pursues his toils,
Nor heeds fierce suns, nor stubborn soils.
Thee oft I met in Hertford's vale,
What time the tuneful nightingale
Recited sweet her solemn song
The beeches and the oaks among:
Upon the banks of Lee reclin'd,
Thy visits sooth'd my pensive mind,

And drove corroding pain away,
And made the rural landscape gay.
How verdant then appear'd the trees!
How grateful was the western breeze!
How sweet the scent of opening flowers!
How fair the hedges and the bowers!
How bright the sun's enlivening beam!
How soft the murmurs of the stream!
Adieu, lov'd vale! adieu, smooth stream!
Yet still, CONTENT! be thou my theme:
'Tis thee, sweet maid! I wooe again,
Attend thy constant lover's strain;
Where-e'er 'tis his the lot to stray,
O deign with him to take thy way!
ODE TO SOLITUDE.
BY THE SAME.

HAIL, silent matron! ever hail!
Thou lover of the wood or vale!
When musing near yon aged tree,

Nor thou despise my numbers rude,
Serious, caelestial SOLITUDE.
Oft in the still retired dell,
Thou hear'st the solemn funeral bell;
Or where the Ascetic's cottage stands,
'Midst cheerless wastes and arid lands;
Oft in the forest's umbrage deep,
Thou yet art seen to sit and weep;
For frequent falls thy tender tear
O'er Youth's cold grave, or Beauty's bier.
Teach me that Life's momentary day,
However various, or how gay,

Is transient as the odorous flower,
That blooms and withers in an hour;
Teach me to aid the suppliant poor,
Nor turn the pilgrim from my door;
For others woes still prompt the sigh,
O parent of Humanity!
Accept these numbers wild and rude,
Caelestial matron! SOLITUDE!

FOND man! retire to this still cell,

Who loves the quiet lone recess,

For pleasures tranquil and serene.
How solemn is the oak's broad shade,
The naked grove seen thro' the glade,
The rock that high projects its steep,
The distant prospect of the deep!
Fond man! here cheerful may'st thou spend
Thy swift-wing'd life, nor fear thy end;
Stealing thro' life, as thro' the plain
Yon rill in murmurs seeks the main.
Here, when the saffron-vested dawn

To these fair groves of venerable shade,
The group of tall elms and the silver spring,
Blame not the man who these his choice has made.
Hast thou not heard, that in a venal age
Wise Scipio from the walls of Rome retir'd;
Content to muse on Nature's simple page,
And scenes the oft'ner view'd, the more admir'd.
Silent, like him, oft let me range the wood,

At morn's inspiring hour, or twilight grey,

ADVICE TO A SHEPHERD.
BY THE SAME.
SHepherd! seek not wealth nor power,
Let the verdant woodbine bower,
And the hills, and vales, and trees,
And the lonely cottage please.
Can the gaudy gilded room
Vie with fields in vernal bloom?
Or Italian airs excel
Plaintive tuneful Philomel?
Can the futile arts of dress

Grace thy modest Shepherdess?
Happier in her humble sphere,
Than the daughters of the peer.
'Midst the city's tempting glare
Dwell Disease, and Strife, and Care:
Quit not then the farm or fold,

ODE ON AUTUMN.
WRITTEN IN THE YEAR MDCCLXI.
BY THE SAME.
ADIEU the pleasing rural scene,
Sequester'd shades and meadows green,
The field thick spread with sheaves of corn,
The walk at early hour of morn.
No linnet's salutary song
Soft echoes now the sprays among:

No nightingale's more plaintive strain
Soothes the lone peasant on the plain.
The vales their chearful green resign,
And on their stems the flowers decline:
No more we wish to pass the hour
Where elms and lilacs form a bower.
And see the swallows leave their home,
To distant, warmer climes they roam;
Where zephyrs cool and grateful showers
Still wake the fair autumnal flowers.
How fade the glories of the year!
They bloom awhile and disappear,
And, melancholy truth, fond man!
Thy life's a flower, thy day's a span.
Parent of All! tremendous Power!
Whom every realm and tongue adore,

Whose mandate form'd earth's spacious plain,
And the immeasurable main.
Prostrate before thy throne we bow,
Author of circling seasons Thou!
O hasten happier days, and bring
One glorious, One Eternal Spring.
EPITAPH ON A PEASANT.
BY THE SAME.
THE Swain who own'd yon rural cot
Now lies near this sequester'd spot.
With his industrious faithful wife
He trod the path of humble life,
Nor knew the sorrows which await
The trifling revels of the great:
Here village lads at evening hour
Shall strew the lately gather'd flower,

And pensive nymphs assemble here,
To shed a sympathetic tear.
O Stranger! thy sad tribute give,
Like Damon die, like Damon live!
For Virtue lasting plaudit gains,
When freed from these terrestrial plains.
PSALM CXXXVII.
BY THE SAME.
WHere the fair streams of fam'd Euphrates stray,
And make the vales of Babylonia gay,
On the green borders of the silver flood,
Judea's exil'd mournful children stood:
A pensive band, opprest with grief severe,
For Zion's fate they shed the frequent tear;
Their silent harps, so tuneful late, unstrung,
High on the branches of the willows hung;

When lo! their enemies demand the strains
That erst resounded sweet on Judah's plains. —
How shall these songs, Jehovah, Sovereign King!
In this strange clime thy captive people sing?
Let my right hand forget the note to play,
Let my mute tongue forget to tune the lay,
If e'er my thought neglectful, faithless roves,
From thee, O Salem! and thy sacred groves:
But, mighty Lord! remember thou their seed,
Who bade thy city mourn, thy people bleed!
Shall not e'er long proud Babel's turrets fall,
And in her fair streets noisome reptiles crawl;
Her haughty warriors pale and breathless lie,
Dash'd on the stones her helpless infants die,
The woes we suffer be to her repaid,
And all her glory sunk in everlasting shade?

THE LATTER PART OF HABBAKUK, CHAPTER III.
BY THE SAME.
THO' in Judea's mead the verdant blade
Nipt by ungenial frost full sudden fade;
Tho' the ripe fig, pride of the garden gay,
Touch'd by the sun's too fervid beam decay;
Tho' fairer vines the raging whirlwind blast,
And olives useless on the heap are cast;
Tho' struck by Death the bleating firstlings fall,
Vacant the fold, untenanted the stall;
Yet still to Thee, Jehovah! Power supreme!
My guide, my only hope, and constant theme!
I lisp the feeble strain, and bow the knee,
And own incessant Strength belongs to Thee!
O let thy Love with rapture fill my breast,
And lead thro' life's untrodden wilds — to Rest.

There's many a strong farmer whose heart would break in two If he could see the townland that we are riding to. Boughs have their fruit and blossom at all times of the year, Rivers are running over with red beer and brown beer, An old man plays the bagpipes in a golden and silver wood, Queens, their eyes blue like the ice, are dancing in a crowd.
Per cruciamina leti Via panditur ardua justis, Et ad astra doloribus itur.
Black is his robe from top to toe, His flesh is white and warm below, All through his silent veins flow free Hunger and thirst and venery, But in his eyes a still small flame Like the first cell from which he came Burns round and luminous, as he rides Singing my song of deicides.
